Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

Let $F:=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Q(q)|\lambda\rangle$ be the charge-$0$ part of
the Fock space of
[[lem-semi-infinite-wedges-are-indexed-by-partitions-and-give-node-action-formulas]],
with basis indexed by all partitions and with the node operators $F_i,E_i$
defined by the stable finite-prefix action. Assign to $|\lambda\rangle$ the
**level-one weight**

$$\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle):=\Lambda_0-\sum_{i\in I}m_i(\lambda)\,\alpha_i, \qquad m_i(\lambda):=\#\{\text{cells of }\lambda\text{ of residue }i\},$$

where the **residue** of a cell in row $r$ and column $c$ is $c-r\bmod e$, and
the **size** $|\lambda|$ is the separate grading. The vacuum is the empty
partition $\varnothing$; $F_i$ adds and $E_i$ removes a node by the explicit
finite node formulas of the same item. The toral action is
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the
addable-minus-removable count, proved to be the Cartan pairing in
[[lem-the-node-count-is-the-level-one-cartan-pairing]], and
$K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$.

A partition is **$e$-regular** if each positive part occurs with multiplicity
$<e$, and **$e$-restricted** if $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}<e$ for every $r\ge1$
(with $\lambda_{r}=0$ beyond the length). These operators are declared linear
endomorphisms here; the affine relations proved later establish the actual
module structure, so nothing about $F$ is silently assumed in this Definition.

Fix an integer $e\ge 2$ and put $I:=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z=\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$
with its cyclic order; elements of $I$ are called **residues**. Let
$A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be the integer matrix with

$$a_{ii}=2,\qquad a_{i,i-1}=a_{i,i+1}=-1\ \ (i\in I)$$

when $e\ge 3$, and with $a_{00}=a_{11}=2$ and the single double edge
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ when $e=2$; all indices are read modulo $e$. Thus for
$e\ge3$ all off-diagonal entries other than the neighbouring entries $-1$ are
$0$, and for $e=2$ the matrix is
$\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Take the diagonal symmetrizer
$D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\dots,1)$ and the quantum parameter $q$ over
$\mathbb Q$, so that $q_i=q^{d_i}=q$ for every $i\in I$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]).

Choose free abelian groups

$$P=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\Lambda_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z\delta, \qquad P^{\vee}=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z h_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z d,$$

with the $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times
P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$ determined by

$$\langle\Lambda_j,h_i\rangle=\delta_{ij},\qquad \langle\delta,h_i\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\Lambda_j,d\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\delta,d\rangle=1 .$$

Define the **simple roots**

$$\alpha_i:=\sum_{j\in I}a_{ji}\Lambda_j+\delta_{i0}\,\delta\qquad(i\in I),$$

let $Q:=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i\subseteq P$ be the **root lattice**
and $Q^+$ its nonnegative cone, and define the **central element**
$c:=\sum_{i\in I}h_i\in P^{\vee}$. The **level** of $\lambda\in P$ is
$\langle c,\lambda\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]),
and the **classical weight lattice** is $P_{\mathrm{cl}}:=P/\mathbb Z\delta$.

The **diagram reflection** $\tau$ is the pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear
involutions $\tau:P\to P$, $P^{\vee}\to P^{\vee}$ with
$\tau(\Lambda_i)=\Lambda_{-i}$, $\tau(\delta)=\delta$, $\tau(h_i)=h_{-i}$ and
$\tau(d)=d$ (indices negated in $\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$).

derivations.claim: The empty partition. The empty partition has exactly one addable node, the cell $(1,1)$ of residue $0$, and no removable nodes; hence $N_i(\varnothing)=\delta_{i0}$. The right-hand side is $\delta_{i0}-\sum_ja_{ij}\cdot0=\delta_{i0}$.

The local step. Let $\mu$ be obtained from $\lambda$ by adding a node $\gamma$ of residue $k$. In $\mu$ the new node $\gamma$ is removable of residue $k$, and the addable/removable status of the other boundary nodes changes exactly at the neighbours of $\gamma$: the node $(r,\lambda_r+1)$ stops being addable and the node $(r+1,\lambda_{r+1})$ stops being removable precisely when they are absorbed or released by the new corner, and their residues are $\lambda_r+1-r$ and $\lambda_{r+1}-(r+1)=k-1$ and $k+1$ shifted by the local geometry, i.e. consecutive to $k$. Bookkeeping the corners of the skew shape $\mu/\lambda$ gives $N_i(\mu)-N_i(\lambda)=-\bigl(2\delta_{ik}-\delta_{i,k-1}-\delta_{i,k+1}\bigr)=-a_{ik}$, and $m_j(\mu)=m_j(\lambda)+\delta_{jk}$; hence the right-hand side changes by $-\sum_ja_{ij}\delta_{jk}=-a_{ik}$ as well, and the identity is preserved.

The identity and its consequences. Induction on the number of cells from step 1.1 with the local step 2.1 gives $N_i(\lambda)=\delta_{i0}-\sum_ja_{ij}m_j(\lambda)$ for every partition. Summing over $i$ and using $\sum_ia_{ij}=0$ and $\sum_i\delta_{i0}=1$ gives $\sum_iN_i(\lambda)=1$. Therefore the toral action $K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ equals $q^{\delta_{i0}-\sum_ja_{ij}m_j}=q^{\langle h_i,\Lambda_0-\sum_jm_j\alpha_j\rangle}$, and the product over $i$ acts by $q^{\sum_iN_i}=q$, so $\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle)=\Lambda_0-\sum_jm_j\alpha_j$ has $\langle c,\mathrm{wt}\rangle=\sum_iN_i=1$ and level one; adding a node of residue $k$ replaces $m_k$ by $m_k+1$, changing the weight by $-\alpha_k$ and $N_i$ by $-a_{ik}$.

Conclusion. The addable-minus-removable count is the level-one Cartan pairing, the sum of the counts is $1$, the central product acts by $q$, and the declared toral action of the partition Fock space is the one required for a level-one module.

The splitting identity. For an addable $i$-node $\gamma$ of $\lambda$, the addable $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are $\{\gamma\}$, the nodes strictly above $\gamma$ in content and those strictly below, and likewise for the removable $i$-nodes; hence, with the two signed counts of the Definition,
$N_i^r(\lambda,\gamma)+N_i^l(\lambda,\gamma)=\bigl(\#\text{addable}_i(\lambda)-1\bigr)-\#\text{removable}_i(\lambda)=N_i(\lambda)-1$,
because $\gamma$ contributes to the addable count but to neither signed count and no removable node equals $\gamma$. The analogous identity holds for a removable node with $\mu$ and $\lambda$ exchanged.

The node formulas are the ones of the stable prefix action. By the content order, the finite-prefix coefficient of an added node is the product of the suffix $K$-weights, which is exactly $q^{N_i^r}$ (each addable $i$-node to the right contributes $+1$, each removable $i$-node to the right contributes $-1$), and for a removed node the renormalised prefix coefficient is $q^{-N_i^l}$ with the smaller diagram $\mu-\gamma$; these are the formulas (38)-(39) of the stable action, restated in the content order.

Calibration at $e=2$. Take $\lambda=(3,1)$. Its cells have contents $0,1,2$ in row $1$ and $-1$ in row $2$, so mod $2$ the residues are $0,1,0,1$. The addable $0$-nodes are $(2,2)$, content $0$, and $(3,1)$, content $-2$; the removable $0$-node is $(1,3)$, content $2$. For $\gamma=(2,2)$: no addable $0$-node lies above content $0$ and the removable node $(1,3)$ does, so $N_0^r=-1$ and the coefficient of $|3,2\rangle$ is $q^{-1}$; for $\gamma=(3,1)$: the addable $(2,2)$ and the removable $(1,3)$ both lie above content $-2$, so $N_0^r=0$ and the coefficient of $|3,1,1\rangle$ is $1$; hence $F_0|3,1\rangle=q^{-1}|3,2\rangle+|3,1,1\rangle$, which is Leclerc's Exercise 15 value. selection: a Chevalley coefficient minimiser is not in general a Kashiwara

where for $F_i$ the counts are taken in the smaller diagram $\lambda$ and count
addable/removable $i$-nodes strictly to the right of the added node (higher
content), and for $E_i$ the counts are taken in the smaller diagram $\mu-\gamma$
and count nodes strictly to the left of the removed node (lower content), with
the removed node excluded; all sums are finite. The toral operators act by
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the
addable-minus-removable count, and $K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$;

For a fixed residue $i$ list the addable and removable $i$-nodes of a partition
**by increasing content** $c-r$; larger content is read as further right or
higher. For an addable $i$-node $\gamma$ of $\lambda$ (so that
$\mu=\lambda+\gamma$) define

derivations.claim: Independence of the $i$-slots. If two $i$-cells are toggled, the neighbours determining each corner's availability are of residues $i\pm1$, and the toggled cell has residue $i$, so it is not a neighbour of any other $i$-cell; hence toggling one $i$-cell never changes the availability of another, every subset of the finitely many slots is realizable, and the orbit is a Boolean cube with $2^k$ distinct partition diagrams.

The cube is the rank-one tensor power. In decreasing-content order, the $j$-th slot's toggling multiplies by $q^{+1}$ or $q^{-1}$ according to occupancy and the iterated coproduct coefficient at slot $j$ is $q^{\sum_{\text{slots before }j}\text{weight}}$ for $f$ and $q^{-\sum_{\text{slots after }j}\text{weight}}$ for $e$; these are exactly $N_i^r$ and $-N_i^l$ by [F3], so the map from tensor bit vectors to partitions is a rank-one module isomorphism onto the cube.

The string rule and lattice stability. Applying the rank-one tensor rule [F2] to the cube and unrolling the strict/non-strict comparison gives: cancel $+-\,$ in decreasing order, then $f$ acts on the first surviving $+$ and $e$ on the last surviving $-$, with zero endpoints when no such sign survives; in increasing order the mirrored statement cancels $-+$ and takes the last $+$ / first $-$. Since all divided powers of order $\ge2$ vanish on each two-vertex factor, every divided $E$- and $F$-power has a Laurent-integral matrix on the cube, so the raw $A_0$-span of partitions is stable under the actual normalized string operators; the standard partition form is the normalized rank-one polarization because it satisfies $(F_i\lambda,\lambda+\gamma)=q^{N_i^r}$ and the adjoint relation transports to the same exponent.

Conclusion. Each fixed-residue orbit is a finite Boolean tensor cube of highest-weight-$1$ strings, the actual normalized string rule is the survivor rule in either content order, including $e=2$, and lattice stability of the raw partition span follows before any congruence is transported.

derivations.claim: The reduction is well defined. The word reduction $-+\to$ empty is the stack matching familiar from bracket sequences: any two adjacent cancellable pairs are either disjoint or share a letter, and the survivors of the stack algorithm do not depend on the order of deletions; equivalently, the unmatched letters are those that are matched by a stack scan, and reversing the word and exchanging $+$ and $-$ exchanges first/last and minus/plus. Hence the good and cogood nodes are well defined by the word alone.

The operator interpretation. By the cube lemma [F1] the actual normalized operators select exactly the survivors: $e_i$ removes the good (first surviving minus) node and $f_i$ adds the cogood (last surviving plus) node, with value $0$ when the respective sign is absent; the equivalent decreasing-content description cancels $+-$ and takes the last surviving $-$ and the first surviving $+$, which is the usual Fayers good-deletion/cogood-addition convention.

Calibrations and the minimiser warning. At $e=3$, $\lambda=(2,1)$ and $i=2$: the addable $2$-nodes are $(1,3)$ and $(2,2)$ in increasing content order, the signature is $++$, so the cogood node is the last plus, the top-right cell $(1,3)$; it is not the leftmost opening $(2,1)$ of a naive minimiser. -\#\{\text{removable }i\text{-nodes of }\lambda\}$ one has

$$N_i(\lambda)=\delta_{i0}-\sum_{j\in I}a_{ij}\,m_j(\lambda),$$

$\sum_{i\in I}N_i(\lambda)=1$; the toral operator acts by

$K_0K_1\cdots K_{e-1}$ acts by $q$, and $\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle)
=\Lambda_0-\sum_jm_j\alpha_j$ has level $1$. In particular
$N_i(\varnothing)=\delta_{i0}$, and adding a node of residue $k$ changes $N_i$
by $-a_{ik}$, hence the weight by $-\alpha_k$.

[[lem-semi-infinite-wedges-are-indexed-by-partitions-and-give-node-action-formulas]],

The mixed commutators. Fix $i
e j$ and a partition $\lambda$. The two colors act on their own corner sets; restricting to the union of the $i$-cube and the $j$-cube through $\lambda$, the two operators move different corners or the same corner in different directions. If the moves commute (different corners) both orders give the same partition and the same product of exponents; if they obstruct each other (adjacent moves sharing a corner) both orders vanish, because the intermediate collision is a repeated-entry wedge; and no configuration produces a nonzero remainder, since the only corners whose availability can change are the two touched cells, whose residues $i
e j$ differ. Hence $[E_i,F_j]=0$ for $i
e j$ on every vector, while $[E_i,F_i]=(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ is the rank-one commutator of [F2].

([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of

with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$

simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, steps
3.1 and 4.1).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

derivations.claim: The vacuum data. By [F1] the vacuum is killed by all $E_i$, is a $K_i$-eigenvector with eigenvalue $q^{\delta_{i0}}$ and a $K_d$-eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$, so $\mathrm{wt}(\varnothing)=\Lambda_0$ by the node-count pairing; in particular the vacuum is a highest weight vector of weight $\Lambda_0$.

Integrability and the highest-vector relations. The nonzero cyclic submodule $M=U_q|\varnothing\rangle$ inherits integrability and the label grading from $F$ by [F2]. Its generator has the highest-vector data of step 1.1, so it meets the integrable highest-vector hypothesis of [F3]. No assertion about the weight of a highest vector in an arbitrary submodule is needed.

Identification and the integral lattice. By [F3] the normalized assignment $v_0\mapsto|\varnothing\rangle$ extends to a homomorphism $V(\Lambda_0)\to M$. It is surjective since the image contains the cyclic generator, and injective since its kernel is a submodule of the simple source and the map is nonzero. Thus $M\cong V(\Lambda_0)$, which proves simplicity as well as the highest weight identification. The divided node operators preserve the partition Laurent lattice: on each finite two-vertex tensor cube this follows from the divided-power coproduct, whose tensor-factor divided powers are integral; hence $U_A^-|\varnothing\rangle$ is an $A$-submodule of that lattice, and it spans $M$ over $\mathbb Q(q)$ because ordinary lower words are scalar multiples of divided lower words. This is the claimed integral lattice.

Conclusion. The vacuum is a highest weight vector of weight $\Lambda_0$, its cyclic submodule is the simple integrable $V(\Lambda_0)$, and the crystal identification with the empty component of the good-node graph is postponed to the crystal theorem rather than asserted here.

citations.quote:
For the declared charge-$0$ node operators and a fixed residue $i$ and partition
$\lambda$, the orbit obtained by toggling the addable/removable $i$-cells of
$\lambda$ is a finite Boolean cube: the availability of one such cell is
unchanged by every other $i$-toggle, including $e=2$. Order the $i$-slots by
decreasing content, call a vertex state $+$ when the slot is occupied (addable)
and $-$ when it is empty (removable), so that the state word records the
configuration. Then the node operators on this cube are exactly the tensor
power $V(1)^{\otimes k}$ of the two-vertex rank-one string with the fixed
coproduct and $K$-exponent $q^{\#+-\#-}$; in particular the raw $A_0$-partition
span is stable under the actual normalized string operators, $f$ applies to the
first surviving $+$ and $e$ to the last surviving $-$ in decreasing-content
order, equivalently $f$ to the last $+$ and $e$ to the first $-$ in
increasing-content order, with $\varepsilon,\varphi$ the surviving minus/plus
counts. The standard partition form is the normalized rank-one polarization,
and all divided $E$- and $F$-powers have Laurent-integral matrices.

The constructed node operators on **all** partition vectors make the charge-$0$
partition Fock space $F$ into a $P$-graded integrable module for
$U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_e)$ with the fixed coproduct and the cyclic Cartan
datum: all toral commutation rules and mixed commutators
$[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ hold, and both quantum Serre
sums vanish, including the cubic $e=2$ case with
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$. Each color acts on finite Boolean
cubes, and $F_i,E_i$ change the $P$-weight by $\mp\alpha_i$. Ordinary standard
coefficients may have $q^{-1}$ poles; normalized Kashiwara lattice stability is
a separate statement.

For every partition $\lambda$, every residue $i\in I$, and
$N_i(\lambda):=\#\{\text{addable }i\text{-nodes of }\lambda\}
-\#\{\text{removable }i\text{-nodes of }\lambda\}$ one has

$$N_i(\lambda)=\delta_{i0}-\sum_{j\in I}a_{ij}\,m_j(\lambda),$$

where $m_j(\lambda)$ is the number of residue-$j$ cells of $\lambda$ and
$A=(a_{ij})$ is the cyclic affine type $A$ Cartan matrix. Consequently
$\sum_{i\in I}N_i(\lambda)=1$; the toral operator acts by
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle=q^{\langle
h_i,\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle)\rangle}$, the central product
$K_0K_1\cdots K_{e-1}$ acts by $q$, and $\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle)
=\Lambda_0-\sum_jm_j\alpha_j$ has level $1$. In particular
$N_i(\varnothing)=\delta_{i0}$, and adding a node of residue $k$ changes $N_i$
by $-a_{ik}$, hence the weight by $-\alpha_k$.

Let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of an integrable chosen $P$-graded type-1 module $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]) with the induced operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ on $L/qL$ ([[def-kashiwara-crystal-operators]]). For $b\in B$ write $\mathrm{wt}(b)=\mu$ when $b\in B_\mu$, and define
$$\varepsilon_i(b):=\max\{n\ge0:\tilde e_i^{\,n}b\neq0\},\qquad \varphi_i(b):=\max\{n\ge0:\tilde f_i^{\,n}b\neq0\}.$$
Then (see below) both numbers are finite and
$$\varphi_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle .$$
The top of the $i$-string through $b$ is the vertex $\tilde e_i^{\,\varepsilon_i(b)}b$, of weight $\mathrm{wt}(b)+\varepsilon_i(b)\alpha_i$; its highest rank-one integer is $\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}(b)\rangle+2\varepsilon_i(b)=\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)$.

In the crystal graph of $(L,B)$ the arrows $b\to\tilde f_ib$ are the inverse raising edges: on an existing edge, $\varepsilon_i$ increases by $1$, $\varphi_i$ decreases by $1$ and the weight decreases by $\alpha_i$, and the $i$-chains of $B$ are the finite strings with $\varepsilon_i(b)+\varphi_i(b)+1$ vertices.

For a crystal basis of the negative half $U_q^-$ ([[thm-the-i-string-decomposition-of-the-negative-half]]) one uses the same arrows and the same finite $\varepsilon_i$, but defines the **formal** $\varphi_i:=\varepsilon_i+\langle h_i,\mathrm{wt}\rangle$ as an integer of the abstract root-graded crystal; it may be negative, and it is not the lowering-chain length. The actual lowering-chain length of a negative-half vertex is denoted $\ell_i^-$ and equals $+\infty$, because $\tilde f_i$ is injective there; the negative half is not asserted to be an integrable finite-string module. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: The crystal basis. By [F1] the $A_0$-span $F_0$ is stable under the normalized string operators, and the mod-$q$ residues of the partition basis are the crystal elements; the string lengths give $\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ as the surviving minus/plus counts, and the weight formula is [F2]. Since each fixed-residue block is a finite tensor cube of two-vertex strings, all crystal axioms (the intertwining of $\varepsilon,\varphi$ with the weight, the partial-inverse property of $e_i,f_i$, and the finiteness of the strings) hold blockwise, hence on the whole graph; the graph has all partitions as vertices because every partition lies in the raw $A_0$-span.

The empty component consists of regular partitions. Use decreasing-content order and the survivor rule. If removing the selected last surviving minus creates $e$ equal rows of length $L-1$, then below its removable row there is a block of $e-1$ rows of length $L-1$ whose last corner is a consecutive same-residue minus: if the upper minus survives, so does this lower one, so the upper one cannot have been selected; hence good deletion preserves regularity. Dually, if adding the selected first surviving plus creates $e$ equal rows of the new length, then a block of $e-1$ rows of that length lies immediately above it and its first addable corner is a consecutive same-residue plus which survives whenever the lower plus does, so the lower plus is not selected; hence cogood addition preserves regularity. Both operators therefore stay inside the regular labels.

Reachability of all regular partitions and the component. Every nonempty regular partition has a top block of $a<e$ equal rows; its first removable corner has residue $L-a$, while the only earlier addable corner has residue $L$, so the minus has no matching same-residue plus and survives: a good deletion exists, it remains regular and lowers the size. Induction on the size together with the inverse axiom reaches every regular partition from the empty one, and since the empty partition is regular and all edges of the component preserve regularity, the empty component is exactly the set of $e$-regular partitions. The transposed ($e$-restricted) model arises by conjugation and is not the same vertex set.

Conclusion. The crystal basis of the whole Fock space is the good-node partition graph on all partitions with the survivor $\varepsilon,\varphi$, and its empty connected component is exactly the $e$-regular partition set, proved by the block argument without an imported path count or an abstract rank-one recognition.

Let $F^{(M)}$ be the charge-$M$ Fock space with ground sequence
$b^\circ_s=u_{M-s}$ and let $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ be the opposite-channel energy.
Then:

(i) **Vanishing against the right tail.** For a fixed type-A ground sequence,
the condition $H_{\mathrm{op}}(b\otimes b^\circ_s)\le0$ means that the added
integer index lies inside or below the filled right tail
$\{M-s,M-s-1,\dots\}$; then $b\wedge b^\circ_s=0$, a sufficiently long finite
prefix of the wedge is already $0$, and hence the element lies in $q^nW_0$ for
every $n$.

(ii) **Dual left tail.** The mirrored condition with the left tail gives the
same exact finite vanishing, with the roles of left and right exchanged.

(iii) **Endomorphisms commuting with the loop.** A nonzero-weight endomorphism
$C$ of $V_{\mathrm{aff}}$ commuting with $z$ has only finitely many
loop-shift/color terms on each fundamental vector; inserting $C$ deep inside a
ground tail is eventually $0$, so it converges $q$-adically to $0$ on every
vector.

(iv) **The period operator.** For the explicit period operator
$T$ on $F^{(M)}$ that prepends $e$ vacuum entries and shifts every old index
down by $e$: $T$ preserves each label-weight/size component, and on the
positive-size-$n$ part its $k$-th power is $0$ as soon as $ke>n$.
Consequently $(1-T)^{-1}=1+T+T^2+\cdots$ is a finite geometric sum on every
nonvacuum weight, and each label weight has only finitely many partition
vectors.

The constructed node operators on **all** partition vectors make the charge-$0$
partition Fock space $F$ into a $P$-graded integrable module for
$U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_e)$ with the fixed coproduct and the cyclic Cartan
datum: all toral commutation rules and mixed commutators
$[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ hold, and both quantum Serre
sums vanish, including the cubic $e=2$ case with
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$. Each color acts on finite Boolean
cubes, and $F_i,E_i$ change the $P$-weight by $\mp\alpha_i$. Ordinary standard
coefficients may have $q^{-1}$ poles; normalized Kashiwara lattice stability is
a separate statement.

Keep the conventions of the charge-$M$ Fock space
[[def-semi-infinite-q-wedge-fock-space-and-q-adic-topology]]. Normal wedges are
bijective with partitions through $i_k=M+\lambda_k-k+1$; in charge $0$ the
vacuum is the empty partition. The stable finite-prefix action defines linear
endomorphisms $F_i,E_i,K_i,K_d$ of $F^{(0)}$ by

$$F_i|\lambda\rangle=\sum_{\text{addable }\gamma\text{ of residue }i}q^{A_i^r-R_i^r}\,|\lambda+\gamma\rangle,\qquad E_i|\mu\rangle=\sum_{\text{removable }\gamma\text{ of residue }i}q^{-(A_i^l-R_i^l)}\,|\mu-\gamma\rangle,$$

where for $F_i$ the counts are taken in the smaller diagram $\lambda$ and count
addable/removable $i$-nodes strictly to the right of the added node (higher
content), and for $E_i$ the counts are taken in the smaller diagram $\mu-\gamma$
and count nodes strictly to the left of the removed node (lower content), with
the removed node excluded; all sums are finite. The toral operators act by
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the
addable-minus-removable count, and $K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$;
the size $|\lambda|$ is a separate grading. Charge $M$ replaces the residues by
content $+M$ and $K_d$ by $\Omega_M(d)-m_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module over $\mathbb Q(q)$ for a finite symmetrizable
Cartan datum such that

(a) $M$ is a weight module with $\dim_{\mathbb Q(q)}M_\mu<\infty$ for every
$\mu\in P$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]);

(b) the weight set $\mathrm{wt}(M)$ is bounded above: it is contained in a
finite union $\bigcup_{j=1}^s(\lambda_j-Q_+)$;

(c) $M$ is integrable, i.e. $E_i$ and $F_i$ act locally nilpotently for every
$i$.

Then $M$ is isomorphic to an algebraic direct sum of simple integrable highest
weight modules $L(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in P^+$
([[thm-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-module-exists-and-is-unique]]);
concretely, every nonzero submodule of $M$ contains a maximal vector $v$ whose
cyclic submodule $U_q(\mathfrak g)v$ is isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$ for some
$\lambda\in P^+$, and $M$ is the direct sum of the submodules generated by the
vectors of any maximal independent family of simple submodules. AC is used
exactly to select a maximal independent family of simple submodules
simultaneously; restricted to any module generated by one finite-dimensional
$U^{\ge0}$-submodule the decomposition is obtained by a finite induction and is
choice-free. The finite-cone modules use the explicit label grading, and the
regularization supplier is used when the original pairing is not separating
([[lem-finite-support-regularization-of-quantum-label-weight-modules]]).

Let $(I,A,D,P,P^{\vee},q)$ be a symmetrizable Cartan datum for a quantum group
with $a_{ii}=2$ for all $i$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]), with root lattice $Q$,
simple roots $\alpha_i\in P$ and integer pairing
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$, and let
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$ be its Drinfeld–Jimbo algebra with generators $E_i,F_i,K_h$
([[def-drinfeld-jimbo-quantized-enveloping-algebra]]). The lattice $P$ plays
the role of the integral weights of the classical theory
([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]); the pairing need not
be perfect, and no identification $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$ is
assumed anywhere.

A **$P$-graded type-one quantum weight module** is a left $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module $M$
together with a direct sum decomposition

$$M=\bigoplus_{\mu\in P}M_\mu$$

(an internal direct sum of $\mathbb Q(q)$-subspaces, only finitely many nonzero
on each vector) such that, for all $\mu\in P$, $h\in P^{\vee}$ and $i\in I$,

$$K_h\ \text{acts on}\ M_\mu\ \text{by the scalar}\ q^{\langle\mu,h\rangle},\qquad E_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu+\alpha_i},\qquad F_iM_\mu\subseteq M_{\mu-\alpha_i}.$$

The subspaces $M_\mu$ are the **chosen label-weight spaces**: the grading is
part of the structure and is not reconstructed from the action, because the
pairing may have a kernel. **Morphisms** of $P$-graded type-one weight modules
are the $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module maps $f\colon M\to N$ with
$f(M_\mu)\subseteq N_\mu$ for every $\mu$; the weight submodules and quotients
considered on this page are those with the induced grading (Verification, steps
3.1 and 4.1).

The module is **integrable** if $E_i$ and $F_i$ are locally nilpotent on every
vector: for every $v\in M$ and every $i$ there are integers $N_e(v,i),N_f(v,i)\ge1$
with $E_i^{N_e(v,i)}v=0$ and $F_i^{N_f(v,i)}v=0$. The exponents may depend on
the vector and on $i$, and both directions are required independently;
integrability is not a uniform nilpotence condition.

The following are additional hypotheses, never part of the definition:
finiteness of the dimension of every $M_\mu$; boundedness of the set of $\mu$
with $M_\mu\ne0$ above (or below); finite generation of $M$. The zero module is
a $P$-graded type-one weight module with the empty grading ($M_\mu=0$ for all
$\mu$), and it is integrable.

Two remarks are recorded here and proved below. First, when the pairing
separates $P$, the spaces $M_\mu$ are exactly the simultaneous eigenspaces of
the $K_h$, and the present definition recovers the usual type-one weight
modules (Verification, steps 2.1 and 4.1). Second, when the pairing does not
separate, distinct labels $\mu\ne\mu'$ may carry the same toral character, and
a simultaneous toral eigenspace must not be equated with a single label space;
the definition therefore takes the label grading as data. The regularization of
finite-cone support and all highest-weight comparisons on this page are proved
later, not assumed here by writing $P=\operatorname{Hom}(P^{\vee},\mathbb Z)$.
No choice principle enters this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Convergence and stabilisation. A coproduct expression applies finitely many generators to the finitely many entries of a prefix; appending the ground tail and using [F1], every term that would need an index at or beyond the cutoff either collides (a repeated entry) or lies in the deep-insertion vanishing range, so the value on any given label is attained on a sufficiently long finite prefix and does not change when the prefix is extended; hence the infinite coproduct sums converge $q$-adically to the stabilized value, which lives in the original space.

The product formula. For a finite prefix $v$ of length $r$ and its charged tail $u=u_{M-r}\wedge u_{M-r-1}\wedge\cdots$, the coproduct splits at the cut with the tail $K$-eigenvalue contributing the boundary scalar; the two terms of the fixed coproduct are exactly $Ev\wedge K_i^{-1}u+v\wedge Eu$ and $Fv\wedge u+K_iv\wedge Fu$, and the boundary scalar is the same on both sides because the tail is a $K$-eigenvector chain; hence the wedge of a prefix with its correctly charged tail is $U_q$-linear. On the vacuum the residue-$M$ single node is created by $F_M$ and killed by all $E_i$, with $K_i$-eigenvalue $q^{\delta_{i\equiv M}}$ by the node-count pairing.

Integrability and decomposition. For a fixed color, [F2] puts each basis vector in a finite two-vertex tensor cube; a vector is a finite linear combination, so both generators of that color are locally nilpotent on it. The charge-$M$ label is $\Omega_M-\sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$, so the support lies in the single downward cone $\Omega_M-Q^+$. Since the simple roots of the full affine datum are independent, a weight fixes all residue counts $m_i$ and hence the size $\sum_i m_i$; only finitely many partitions have that size, proving finite-dimensional label spaces. Thus all the finite-cone and finite-weight hypotheses of [F3] hold, and $F$ is a locally weight-finite direct sum of simple integrable highest weight modules. Choice enters only through [F3]. Characters and multiplicities are computed later from the actual crystal highest vertices.

Conclusion. The stable prefix operators give a well-defined integrable affine action on the charge-$M$ Fock space with the displayed wedge product formulas, $q$-adic convergence and finite stabilisation, and the finite-weight upper cone is a locally weight-finite direct sum of simple integrable highest weight modules, with the Axiom of Choice used only as declared.

citations.quote:
The whole level-one Fock module has the crystal basis $(F_0,B_F)$ with
$F_0=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Z[q]|\lambda\rangle$ and
$B_F=\{|\lambda\rangle+qF_0:\lambda\text{ a partition}\}$. The normalized
Kashiwara operators remove the good normal $i$-node and add the cogood conormal
$i$-node of the corrected signature of
[[def-good-and-cogood-nodes-by-residue-signature-reduction]], and
$\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are the surviving minus/plus counts. The graph is a
graph on all partitions, not only regular ones; its empty connected component
is precisely the set of $e$-regular partitions, while the $e$-restricted labels
belong to the transposed model. A pole or a unique Chevalley term does not
determine a crystal arrow.

In the charge-$0$ partition Fock space the vacuum $\varnothing$ has
$E_i\varnothing=0$, $K_i\varnothing=q^{\delta_{i0}}\varnothing$ and
$K_d\varnothing=\varnothing$, so its weight is $\Lambda_0$. The nonzero cyclic
submodule $M:=U_q(\mathfrak g)|\varnothing\rangle$ is the simple integrable
highest weight module $V(\Lambda_0)$; its integral lattice is
$U_A^-|\varnothing\rangle$ for $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$, and its crystal is the
empty graph component, identified in
[[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]]
rather than equated with the module.

**Assume the axiom of choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $M$ be a chosen $P$-graded type-one quantum weight module that is integrable, has finite-dimensional label-weight spaces and weight set contained in a finite union of cones $\lambda-Q_+$ ([[def-quantum-weight-module-and-integrability]]), and let $(L,B)$ be a crystal basis of $M$ ([[def-crystal-lattice-and-crystal-basis]]).

(i) **Splitting along the top isotypic part.** Let $\lambda$ be a maximal weight of $M$, put $N_0:=U_q(\mathfrak g)M_\lambda$ and let $N_1$ be the sum of the remaining simple constituents, so that $M=N_0\oplus N_1$ and $N_0\cong V(\lambda)^{\oplus m}$ with $m=\dim M_\lambda$. Then $L=(L\cap N_0)\oplus(L\cap N_1)$, $B=\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_0)/q(L\cap N_0)\bigr)\sqcup\bigl(B\cap(L\cap N_1)/q(L\cap N_1)\bigr)$, and both pairs are crystal bases of $N_0$ and $N_1$.

(ii) **Uniqueness.** There is a locally weight-finite indexed family $(\lambda_j)_{j\in J}$ in $P^+$ and an isomorphism of $U_q(\mathfrak g)$-modules $\Phi:M\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{j\in J}V(\lambda_j)$ with $\Phi(L)=\bigoplus_j\mathcal L(\lambda_j)$ and $\Phi$ inducing a bijection $B\to\bigsqcup_j\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$ of crystals. The multiset $\{\lambda_j:j\in J\}$ is the multiset of highest weights of the simple integrable constituents of $M$: the number of $j$ with $\lambda_j=\lambda$ equals the multiplicity $[M:V(\lambda)]$.

(iii) **Components.** Through $\Phi$ the connected components of the crystal $B$ are exactly the canonical highest weight crystals $\mathcal B(\lambda_j)$; each component has a unique highest weight element $b$, of dominant weight $\lambda$, and equals the lowering-generated subcrystal $F(b)$ of [[def-highest-weight-element-and-connected-highest-weight-crystal]]. In particular the crystal graph of any crystal basis of $M$ is determined up to isomorphism by $M$, and no other highest weight elements occur.

**Choice.** The axiom of choice is declared in [[def-axiom-of-choice]] and used to obtain the decomposition of $M$ into simple integrable highest weight modules from [[prop-integrable-quantum-highest-weight-modules-are-semisimple]], which selects bases of the finite-dimensional maximal-vector spaces simultaneously. It also permits simultaneous choices of lifts of the finite residue bases in the possibly infinite family of top spaces. After those choices, each lattice and crystal argument is finite and choice-free. No incompatible-axiom branch is used, and no global $\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness is assumed. The index set $J$ need not be finite in affine or indefinite type; local weight finiteness means only finitely many summands contribute to any fixed label-weight space.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The $\Lambda_0$ isotypic part. The weight $\Lambda_0$ weight space of $F$ is one-dimensional, spanned by the vacuum; since $\Lambda_0$ is a maximal weight, the top isotypic submodule is generated by the vacuum and equals the simple module $M=V(\Lambda_0)$ by [F2], whose crystal is the empty component $B(\Lambda_0)$ by [F1].

The other highest vertices. Read the signature top-to-bottom in decreasing content. For the top block of $a$ equal rows of length $L$, the only earlier plus has residue $L$ and its matching removable minus has residue $L-a$; if all minuses are cancelled then $e$ divides $a$ (otherwise the last minus of the block survives unmatched). Cancelling the block's matching pair and repeating with each next block shows that the highest crystal vertices are exactly the partitions obtained by repeating each row of an ordinary partition $\rho$ exactly $e$ times; each residue occurs $|\rho|$ times, so the weight is $\Lambda_0-|\rho|\delta$, and there are $p(k)$ such labels of weight $\Lambda_0-k\delta$.

The decomposition. The full Fock module has finite label spaces and support in $\Lambda_0-Q^+$, so [F3] applies and identifies the field constituents of the highest crystal labels of step 1.2; combined with step 1.1 this gives $F=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)}$ as a locally weight-finite indexed sum, and taking characters gives the displayed product formula. The raw standard vectors attached to the non-regular highest labels are not asserted to be field-highest vectors, and the ambient basis is not asserted to be component-compatible.

Conclusion. The empty component is the canonical $B(\Lambda_0)$ with the $e$-regular labels, its module and lower lattice are $M$ and $M\cap F_0$, it occurs once, and the full decomposition has $p(k)$ copies of $V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)$, with the Axiom of Choice used only through the declared decomposition [F3].

boundaries.evidence: The empty partition is the anchor of the involution: by definition it maps to itself, and step 1.1's path-based construction starts from that anchor, consistent with the fixed fundamental weight.

The identity and exponent-zero cases are checked: step 1.1 verifies the recursion along a lowering path together with the fixed empty label, and step 2.1 shows the weight compatibility holds for all weights including those with a zero coefficient.

The base of the path definition is the one-step case: step 1.1 defines the involution by negating all colors along any lowering path and proves well-definedness, with the empty path giving the fixed label.

The degenerate case of comparing the two models is exactly what is separated: step 3.1 shows conjugation is a dictionary between the regular and restricted models rather than a self-map, so no identification of the same-model involution with conjugation is assumed.

The two endpoints of a lowering path are both specified: the involution starts at the empty label and negates colors at each step, so its value is determined by the path's endpoints, as step 1.1 verifies.
Well-definedness independent of the chosen path is proved in step 1.1, so the definition does not rely on selecting a path, and no other selection occurs.

boundaries.reason: The item fixes conventions and proves well-definedness; it asserts no biconditional between conditions, only identities and a dictionary between two models.
No converse direction is owed: the statements are a definition of one involution and a comparison theorem, neither phrased as an if-and-only-if.

citations.quote:
With the declared use of the Axiom of Choice in the general integrable-module
decomposition, the empty connected component of the full partition crystal of
[[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]] is
the canonical highest weight crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with exactly the
$e$-regular labels. Its module is $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)|\varnothing\rangle$ and
its lower $A_0$-lattice is $M\cap F_0$; it occurs once. More precisely

$$F=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)},$$

a locally weight-finite indexed direct sum in which $p(k)$ is the number of
ordinary partitions of $k$; consequently
$\mathrm{ch}\,F=\mathrm{ch}\,V(\Lambda_0)\prod_{r\ge1}(1-e^{-r\delta})^{-1}$.
A highest **crystal** label need not be a highest **field** standard vector, and
the ambient canonical basis need not split these summands.

The whole level-one Fock module has the crystal basis $(F_0,B_F)$ with
$F_0=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Z[q]|\lambda\rangle$ and
$B_F=\{|\lambda\rangle+qF_0:\lambda\text{ a partition}\}$. The normalized
Kashiwara operators remove the good normal $i$-node and add the cogood conormal
$i$-node of the corrected signature of
[[def-good-and-cogood-nodes-by-residue-signature-reduction]], and
$\varepsilon_i,\varphi_i$ are the surviving minus/plus counts. The graph is a
graph on all partitions, not only regular ones; its empty connected component
is precisely the set of $e$-regular partitions, while the $e$-restricted labels
belong to the transposed model. A pole or a unique Chevalley term does not
determine a crystal arrow.

Fix an integer $e\ge 2$ and put $I:=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z=\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$
with its cyclic order; elements of $I$ are called **residues**. Let
$A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be the integer matrix with

$$a_{ii}=2,\qquad a_{i,i-1}=a_{i,i+1}=-1\ \ (i\in I)$$

when $e\ge 3$, and with $a_{00}=a_{11}=2$ and the single double edge
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ when $e=2$; all indices are read modulo $e$. Thus for
$e\ge3$ all off-diagonal entries other than the neighbouring entries $-1$ are
$0$, and for $e=2$ the matrix is
$\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Take the diagonal symmetrizer
$D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\dots,1)$ and the quantum parameter $q$ over
$\mathbb Q$, so that $q_i=q^{d_i}=q$ for every $i\in I$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]).

Choose free abelian groups

$$P=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\Lambda_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z\delta, \qquad P^{\vee}=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z h_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z d,$$

with the $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times
P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$ determined by

$$\langle\Lambda_j,h_i\rangle=\delta_{ij},\qquad \langle\delta,h_i\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\Lambda_j,d\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\delta,d\rangle=1 .$$

Define the **simple roots**

$$\alpha_i:=\sum_{j\in I}a_{ji}\Lambda_j+\delta_{i0}\,\delta\qquad(i\in I),$$

let $Q:=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i\subseteq P$ be the **root lattice**
and $Q^+$ its nonnegative cone, and define the **central element**
$c:=\sum_{i\in I}h_i\in P^{\vee}$. The **level** of $\lambda\in P$ is
$\langle c,\lambda\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]),
and the **classical weight lattice** is $P_{\mathrm{cl}}:=P/\mathbb Z\delta$.

The **diagram reflection** $\tau$ is the pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear
involutions $\tau:P\to P$, $P^{\vee}\to P^{\vee}$ with
$\tau(\Lambda_i)=\Lambda_{-i}$, $\tau(\delta)=\delta$, $\tau(h_i)=h_{-i}$ and
$\tau(d)=d$ (indices negated in $\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$).

Let $\lambda\in P$ be a dominant integral label weight, put
$m_i:=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\ge0$, and let $M(\lambda)$ be the quantum Verma
module with highest vector $v_\lambda$
([[def-quantum-verma-module-and-simple-highest-weight-quotient]],
[[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]).

(i) The quotient $\tilde L(\lambda):=M(\lambda)/\sum_iU_q(\mathfrak g)F_i^{(m_i+1)}v_\lambda$
is nonzero, has finite-dimensional label weights and support
$\lambda-Q_+$, is integrable, and equals the canonical simple highest weight
module $L(\lambda)$, which is simple also as an ordinary (not assumed graded)
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module.

(ii) **Universality.** Every integrable cyclic highest weight module $V$ of
highest weight $\lambda$ with highest vector $v\ne0$ receives a
$U_q(\mathfrak g)$-module map $\tilde L(\lambda)\to V$ with
$\bar v_\lambda\mapsto v$, and this map is unique; every nonzero such $V$ is
isomorphic to $L(\lambda)$.

(iii) Its character equals the classical integrable highest weight character of
the explicitly regularized realization of the datum. No global
$\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-freeness and no crystal or global basis is used.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

Fix a residue $i$ and a partition $\lambda$, and write the **signature** of
$\lambda$ at $i$ as the word in the symbols $+$ (addable $i$-node) and $-$
(removable $i$-node) whose letters are the addable and removable $i$-nodes of
$\lambda$ read in the fixed increasing-content order of
[[def-the-node-order-and-n-i-exponents-for-fock-space]]. Reduce the word by
cancelling adjacent pairs $-+$ as long as such a pair remains. The surviving
minus letters are called **normal removable** $i$-nodes, and the first surviving
minus is the **good node** of $\lambda$ for $e_i$; the surviving plus letters
are called **conormal addable** $i$-nodes, and the last surviving plus is the
**cogood node** for $f_i$. If no sign of the required type survives, the
corresponding operator is $0$ on $|\lambda\rangle$. Equivalently, reading the
signature in decreasing content with the reversed symbols, one cancels $+-$
and takes the good node as the last surviving $-$ and the cogood node as the
first surviving $+$.

derivations.claim: Well-definedness and involution. Let $v_0$ be the normalized highest vector. Twist $V(\Lambda_0)$ by the diagram automorphism $\tau$; the defining relations are preserved and the twisted highest weight is again $\Lambda_0$, so the uniqueness in [F2] gives a $\mathbb Q(q)$-linear map $J_\tau$ with $J_\tau v_0=v_0$ and $J_\tau(xv)=\tau(x)J_\tau(v)$. Its square is a module map fixing the cyclic generator, hence is the identity. The unique $i$-string decomposition is carried to the $-i$-string decomposition, so $J_\tau\tilde f_i=\tilde f_{-i}J_\tau$ and likewise for $\tilde e_i$. The canonical $A_0$-lattice is the span of the iterated Kashiwara lowering words on $v_0$, not the span of ordinary divided-generator words ([[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-exists]]); therefore $J_\tau$ preserves that lattice and its crystal residue set. Its induced involution is $M$. Applying this fixed residue map to any lowering path proves path independence.

Weight compatibility. Since $\tau(\Lambda_0)=\Lambda_0$, $\tau(\delta)=\delta$ and $\tau(\alpha_i)=\alpha_{-i}$, the involution satisfies $\mathrm{wt}\,M=\tau(\mathrm{wt})$, and it is an involution of the regular label set; no affine longest element formula is used.

Conjugation versus Mullineux. By [F3] conjugation sends residue $i$ to $-i$ and compares the regular and restricted models, so it is a model dictionary rather than a self-map of the regular set: for $e\ge3$ the conjugate of a regular partition is generally restricted and not regular, and for $e=2$ the reflection acts trivially while conjugation changes partitions visibly, so the two maps are distinct. The restricted sign involution $CMC^{-1}$ is the transport of $M$, and dominance on equal-size partitions is the published prefix-sum order, reversed by conjugation; horizontal-strip inclusion is not dominance.

Conclusion. Regular means part multiplicities $<e$, restricted means adjacent differences $<e$, conjugation is the regular/restricted comparison sending $i$ to $-i$, and the Mullineux involution $M$ is the well-defined same-model involution obtained from the datum reflection with weight action $\tau$, distinct from both conjugation and the adjoint transpose.

boundaries.evidence: The vacuum is the base of the triangular system: step 1.1's fixed-point equations start at the empty partition with the vacuum basis vector, which the ambient bar fixes.

Zero entries are handled: step 1.1's system has diagonal one and off-diagonal coefficients in the ideal generated by q with strictly dominated rows, so entries may vanish, as the degree-four matrix shows, without breaking the recursion.

The coefficient-one normalization is checked: the diagonal of the triangular system is one in step 1.1, and step 3.1 shows exactly the regular global basis elements form the lower basis of the basic module through the two suppliers.

The degenerate failure of the transpose symmetry is pinned: step 4.1 exhibits the coefficient of the partition with two ones and a two in the highest degree-four label equal to q against a vanishing coefficient of the column partition, so the accidental low-degree symmetry fails at the first degenerate configuration.

The two ends of the dominance chain are covered: step 1.1 solves from the most dominant label downward, and step 2.1 proves prefix independence by moving a new minimum through the prefix at the other end of the index line.

The bar is an explicit semi-infinite wedge map and the corrections are solved by finite triangularity; the only choice-dependent input is the declared use of the lower-global suppliers, and this item makes no selection of its own. The Statement's explicit wedge bar and the finite triangularity of the recursion carry the construction.

boundaries.reason: The theorem establishes triangularity, integrality and the identification of the basic lower basis; no biconditional is asserted, so the forward axis is not engaged.
No converse is claimed: the statements are existence and uniqueness of the triangular family and a negative symmetry counterexample, not an if-and-only-if requiring a reverse proof.

citations.quote:
For $N\ge1$ let $V_{\mathrm{aff}}^{\otimes N}$ carry the affine Hecke action and put
$W_N:=V_{\mathrm{aff}}^{\otimes N}\big/\ker A_N$, where $A_N=\sum_{w\in S_N}S_w$;
write $u_{m_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge u_{m_N}$ for the image of the pure tensor, and let
$\wedge$ denote this product. Call an index tuple **normal** (or normally
ordered) if $m_1>m_2>\cdots>m_N$, and set $W_A:=\sum_{\text{normal }I}\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]\,u_I$,
$W_0:=\bigoplus_{\text{normal }I}\mathbb Z[q]\,u_I$, where $u_I$ is the image of
the corresponding ordered wedge.

For $l<m$ write $m-l=ae+b$ with $a\ge0$, $0\le b<e$ (so $a=\lfloor(m-l)/e\rfloor$
and $b$ is the residue difference). The **normal-ordering relations** are:

$$u_l\wedge u_l=0;\qquad u_l\wedge u_m=-u_m\wedge u_l\quad(b=0);\qquad u_l\wedge u_m=-q^{-1}u_m\wedge u_l\quad(a=0,\ b>0);$$

$$u_l\wedge u_m=-q^{-1}u_m\wedge u_l-u_{l+ae}\wedge u_{m-ae}-q^{-1}u_{m-ae}\wedge u_{l+ae}\quad(a>0,\ b>0),$$

where the last line is to be read as a relation in $W_N$ and is applied
recursively to its two remaining unordered pairs; each recursion step strictly
decreases the gap of the unordered pair it rewrites and keeps every index
between $l$ and $m$, so the procedure terminates. The energy normal order is
the equivalent formulation through the opposite-channel energy:
$u_{m_1}\wedge u_{m_2}$ is rewritten toward decreasing indices by
$H_{\mathrm{op}}(u_{m_1}\otimes u_{m_2})>0\iff m_1>m_2$ of
[[def-the-level-one-vector-representation-its-affinization-and-energy-function]].

For every $N\ge1$ the normally ordered wedges
$\{u_{m_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge u_{m_N}:m_1>m_2>\cdots>m_N\}$ of
[[def-finite-q-wedge-space-and-normal-ordering-relations]] form a
$\mathbb Q(q)$-basis of $W_N$ and an $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$-basis of the
Laurent lattice $W_A$. The straightening algorithm terminates with a
well-founded profile: the total index sum and the ambient index interval are
preserved, secondary pairs become strictly more balanced in the sorted
dominance profile, and a leading adjacent swap decreases the inversion count;
in particular no bound by the initial inversion count alone is used. The
$A_0$-chart $W_0$ spanned by the normal wedges with $\mathbb Z[q]$ coefficients
is a crystal basis: for each color $i$, on the occupied set of a normal tuple
the disjoint pairs $(u_{i+ke},u_{i+ke+1})$ behave as two-vertex highest-weight
$1$ strings, empty and doubly occupied pairs are frozen, and a shift of an
index by one either stays ordered or collides to zero; hence the residues of
the ordered wedges are stable under the normalized string operators and give a
crystal of the integrable affine wedge module. The image of the full
$\mathbb Z[q]$-tensor lattice need not equal $W_0$, and negative powers of $q$
in the straightening are not asserted to be triangular at $q=0$.

Let $F^{(M)}$ be the charge-$M$ Fock space with ground sequence
$b^\circ_s=u_{M-s}$ and let $H_{\mathrm{op}}$ be the opposite-channel energy.
Then:

(i) **Vanishing against the right tail.** For a fixed type-A ground sequence,
the condition $H_{\mathrm{op}}(b\otimes b^\circ_s)\le0$ means that the added
integer index lies inside or below the filled right tail
$\{M-s,M-s-1,\dots\}$; then $b\wedge b^\circ_s=0$, a sufficiently long finite
prefix of the wedge is already $0$, and hence the element lies in $q^nW_0$ for
every $n$.

(ii) **Dual left tail.** The mirrored condition with the left tail gives the
same exact finite vanishing, with the roles of left and right exchanged.

(iii) **Endomorphisms commuting with the loop.** A nonzero-weight endomorphism
$C$ of $V_{\mathrm{aff}}$ commuting with $z$ has only finitely many
loop-shift/color terms on each fundamental vector; inserting $C$ deep inside a
ground tail is eventually $0$, so it converges $q$-adically to $0$ on every
vector.

(iv) **The period operator.** For the explicit period operator
$T$ on $F^{(M)}$ that prepends $e$ vacuum entries and shifts every old index
down by $e$: $T$ preserves each label-weight/size component, and on the
positive-size-$n$ part its $k$-th power is $0$ as soon as $ke>n$.
Consequently $(1-T)^{-1}=1+T+T^2+\cdots$ is a finite geometric sum on every
nonvacuum weight, and each label weight has only finitely many partition
vectors.

For the declared charge-$0$ node operators and a fixed residue $i$ and partition
$\lambda$, the orbit obtained by toggling the addable/removable $i$-cells of
$\lambda$ is a finite Boolean cube: the availability of one such cell is
unchanged by every other $i$-toggle, including $e=2$. Order the $i$-slots by
decreasing content, call a vertex state $+$ when the slot is occupied (addable)
and $-$ when it is empty (removable), so that the state word records the
configuration. Then the node operators on this cube are exactly the tensor
power $V(1)^{\otimes k}$ of the two-vertex rank-one string with the fixed
coproduct and $K$-exponent $q^{\#+-\#-}$; in particular the raw $A_0$-partition
span is stable under the actual normalized string operators, $f$ applies to the
first surviving $+$ and $e$ to the last surviving $-$ in decreasing-content
order, equivalently $f$ to the last $+$ and $e$ to the first $-$ in
increasing-content order, with $\varepsilon,\varphi$ the surviving minus/plus
counts. The standard partition form is the normalized rank-one polarization,
and all divided $E$- and $F$-powers have Laurent-integral matrices.

Let $M_A$ be $U_A^-$ or $V_A(\lambda)=U_A^-v_\lambda$, let $L$ be $\mathcal L(\infty)$ or $\mathcal L(\lambda)$, let $L^-:=\psi(L)$ be the bar lattice, all as in [[def-the-bar-lattice-and-integral-lattice-of-a-based-module]] and [[def-integral-residue-lattices-of-the-negative-half-and-highest-weight-modules]], and let $E_{\mathbb Z}:=M_A\cap L\cap L^-$ be the balanced intersection. Let $\mathcal B$ be $\mathcal B(\infty)$ or $\mathcal B(\lambda)$.

By [[thm-the-highest-weight-crystal-triple-is-balanced]] the integral triple $(M_A,L,L^-)$ is balanced componentwise: for every root or label degree the canonical map $E_{\mathbb Z}\to(M_A\cap L)/(M_A\cap qL)$ is an isomorphism onto the free $\mathbb Z$-span $\bigoplus_{b\in\mathcal B}\mathbb Zb$ of the crystal classes of that degree. For $b\in\mathcal B$ define the **lower global lift** $G(b)$ to be the unique element of $E_{\mathbb Z}$ whose residue class in $(M_A\cap L)/(M_A\cap qL)$ is $b$. The family $G(\mathcal B)$ is the **lower global basis** of $M_A$ (of $U_A^-$ or of $V_A(\lambda)$).

With these definitions, the theorem's extensions give the basis assertions: the $A$-span of $G(\mathcal B)$ is $M_A$, its $A_0$-span is $L$, its $A_\infty$-span is $L^-$, and its $\mathbb Z$-span is $E_{\mathbb Z}$, while after tensoring with $\mathbb Q$ the residue classes of the $G(b)$ are the full rational crystal spaces; in particular $G(\mathcal B)$ is an $A$-basis of $M_A$. Each $G(b)$ is bar fixed, $G(0)$ is not defined, and no equality of $E_{\mathbb Z}$ with the whole Laurent module $M_A$ is implied; the identification of the integral residue subgroup with $\mathbb Z\mathcal B(\lambda)$ for highest modules is the corresponding part of the same theorem. The lifts are characterized by the simultaneous balanced intersection, not by an unproved unitriangular word-basis condition, and all definitions apply componentwise on finite root or label components and are extended by their direct sums.

For the divided-power integral form $U_A^-$ of [[def-lusztig-divided-power-integral-form]] and for every dominant $\lambda$, let $M_A$ be $U_A^-$ or $V_A(\lambda)=U_A^-v_\lambda$, let $L$ be $\mathcal L(\infty)$ or $\mathcal L(\lambda)$ with bar lattice $L^-=\psi(L)$, and let $\mathcal B$ be $\mathcal B(\infty)$ or $\mathcal B(\lambda)$. Then there is a unique lower global family $G(\mathcal B)\subseteq M_A\cap L\cap L^-$ with the property that the residue class of $G(b)$ in $(M_A\cap L)/(M_A\cap qL)$ is $b$ for every $b\in\mathcal B$, namely the family of [[def-lower-global-basis-of-a-quantum-highest-weight-module]]. It is bar invariant, a genuine $A=\mathbb Z[q,q^{-1}]$ basis of $M_A$, and a basis of both rational chart lattices $L$ and $L^-$ over $A_0$ and $A_\infty$; its $\mathbb Z$-span is the simultaneous balanced intersection $M_A\cap L\cap L^-$ and its field span is the whole module. It is adapted to every divided string-image ideal in the exact sense of the integral balanced theorem, and the same family is obtained with residue $b$ over either chart. No word family is assumed to be a basis, no unitriangular characterization is used, and no lower lattice self-duality is asserted.

With the declared use of the Axiom of Choice in the general integrable-module
decomposition, the empty connected component of the full partition crystal of
[[thm-the-crystal-of-level-one-fock-space-is-the-good-node-partition-graph]] is
the canonical highest weight crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$, with exactly the
$e$-regular labels. Its module is $M=U_q(\mathfrak g)|\varnothing\rangle$ and
its lower $A_0$-lattice is $M\cap F_0$; it occurs once. More precisely

$$F=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}V(\Lambda_0-k\delta)^{\oplus p(k)},$$

a locally weight-finite indexed direct sum in which $p(k)$ is the number of
ordinary partitions of $k$; consequently
$\mathrm{ch}\,F=\mathrm{ch}\,V(\Lambda_0)\prod_{r\ge1}(1-e^{-r\delta})^{-1}$.
A highest **crystal** label need not be a highest **field** standard vector, and
the ambient canonical basis need not split these summands.

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.

**Partitions.** Let $n\ge 0$ be an integer. A **partition of $n$** is a finite
weakly decreasing sequence $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ of positive
integers with $\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k=n$. Its entries are the **parts** of
$\lambda$ and $k$ is the **number of parts**. For $n=0$ the only partition is
the **empty partition** $\varnothing$, the empty sequence with $k=0$; for
$n\ge 1$ one has $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_k\ge 1$ and
$k\le n$. We write $\lambda\vdash n$. Trailing zeros are not parts: a finite
sequence of nonnegative integers ending in $0$ is not a partition, so the
number of parts of $\lambda$ is determined by $\lambda$ and
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$ is a different data type from
$(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k,0)$.

**English Young diagrams.** The **(English) Young diagram** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$[\lambda]:=\{\,(i,j)\;:\;1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le \lambda_i\,\}\subseteq\mathbb N\times\mathbb N,$$
where $i$ numbers the **rows** downward and $j$ numbers the **columns**
rightward. An element of $[\lambda]$ is a **node**, or box, of the diagram. Row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ carries $\lambda_i$ nodes, and column $j$ carries
$$\lambda'_j:=\#\{\,i: \lambda_i\ge j\,\}$$
nodes, a quantity that is $0$ beyond the last column (and for every $j\ge1$ when $\lambda=\varnothing$). Since a partition is weakly
decreasing, $[\lambda]$ determines $\lambda$: if $[\mu]=[\lambda]$, then row
$i$ of $[\lambda]$ is row $i$ of $[\mu]$, so $\mu_i=\lambda_i$ for every $i$
and $\mu=\lambda$. In particular $[\varnothing]=\emptyset$, the empty diagram.

**Conjugation.** The **conjugate partition** of a nonempty $\lambda$ is
$$\lambda':=(\lambda'_1,\lambda'_2,\dots,\lambda'_{\lambda_1}),$$
the sequence of column heights of $[\lambda]$, with $\varnothing':=\varnothing$
for the empty partition. This is again a partition of $n$, and
$[\lambda']$ is the transpose of $[\lambda]$:
for $1\le i\le\lambda_1$ and $1\le j\le k$,
$$(i,j)\in[\lambda']\iff j\le\lambda'_i\iff \lambda_j\ge i\iff (j,i)\in[\lambda].$$
Outside these bounds neither diagram contains the corresponding node; for the empty partition both diagrams are empty.
Conjugation is an involution, $\lambda''=\lambda$, because
$\lambda''_i=\#\{j:\lambda'_j\ge i\}$ counts the columns of $[\lambda]$ of
height at least $i$, that is, the columns $j$ with at least $i$ rows of length
$\ge j$, which by weak decrease is exactly the set of $j\le\lambda_i$. Thus
$\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is a bijection on the partitions of $n$, exchanging
the number of parts with the largest part for nonempty partitions.

**Size zero.** The symmetric group of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is
$S_n:=\operatorname{Sym}(\{1,\dots,n\})$ ([[def-symmetric-group]]) for every
$n\ge 0$, and we fix
$$S_0:=\operatorname{Sym}(\emptyset)=\{1\},$$
the trivial group; for $n=0$ the set $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is empty and the group
acts trivially on every size-zero object below. This is the convention used
whenever the constructions of this page are read at $n=0$.

A partition is **regular** if each positive part occurs with multiplicity $<e$,
and **restricted** if $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}<e$ for every $r$. Conjugation
$C:\lambda\mapsto\lambda'$ is the comparison map between the regular and the
restricted models; it sends the residue $i$ to $-i$. It is **not** the
same-model sign involution.

On the regular basic crystal of
[[thm-the-empty-component-is-the-highest-weight-crystal-b-lambda-zero]] define
$M$ by negating all colors of a lowering path from the empty partition:
$M(f_ib)=f_{-i}M(b)$ for every edge, $M(\varnothing)=\varnothing$. The
restricted sign involution is the conjugate $CMC^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: Integral dominance triangularity. On each finite degree the equations $\psi(G(\lambda))=G(\lambda)$ form a finite triangular semilinear system with diagonal $1$; solving from the leading term downwards, the residual $f+\bar f$ is antisymmetric under the bar and its unique positive-$q$ part gives the next correction, so $d_{\mu,\lambda}\in q\mathbb Z[q]$, vanishes unless $\mu$ is strictly dominated by $\lambda$, and preserves the residue multiset (same $e$-core) because every straightening step preserves residues.

Prefix independence and the charts. Let $m$ exceed the partition size and move a new minimum $u_{-m}$ through the prefix. Every secondary correction removes that minimum and leaves $m+1$ indices above $-m$ with total sum bounded by the ground sum plus size minus $m$, which is smaller than the minimum possible sum of $m+1$ distinct integers above $-m$; hence all secondary branches vanish by [F2], only the leading factor $(-1)^mq^{-\#\text{unequal}}$ survives, and it cancels the new normalization. Therefore $\psi$ and the corrections are prefix-independent, giving the actual infinity chart and the balanced $\mathbb Z$-intersection; $F_A,F_0$ and the integral chart are kept separate.

The basic lower basis. On $M$ the $A$-lattice of divided node actions maps into the partition $A$-lattice because the cube matrices are Laurent-integral; its lower lattice maps into $F_0$, and the lower global basis of [F3] is bar-fixed with regular crystal residues. By the balanced-triple uniqueness of [F3] the images agree with the unique ambient $G$'s of the regular degree, so every $e$-regular $G(\lambda)$ lies in $M$ and the regular family is the lower global basis of $M$; no integral splitting or saturation is assumed, and the ambient basis is not claimed component-compatible.

The false transpose symmetry. The equality $d_{\lambda,\mu}=d_{\mu',\lambda'}$ fails at $e=2$ and degree $4$: the recursion gives $d_{(2,1,1),(4)}=q$ while $d_{(1,1,1,1),(3,1)}=0$, since $(2,1,1)'=(3,1)$ and $4'=(1,1,1,1)$; the source symmetry statement concerns the bar transition matrix, not the lower matrix $D$. Ambient natural-form dual coefficients use $(D^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$, and basic upper coefficients need the restricted Gram inverse, which may have rational entries.

Conclusion. The explicit wedge bar is involutive, prefix-independent and integral; the global basis $G(\lambda)$ is dominance-unitriangular with $q\mathbb Z[q]$ off-diagonal coefficients and same-core support, the $A$-and $A_0$-bases and the balanced intersection are as displayed, exactly the regular family is the lower global basis of $M=V(\Lambda_0)$, and the naive transpose symmetry of $D$ is false while the correct inverse/Gram rules hold.
